properties.speed_source: estimated typical light-rail operating speed through the downtown subway, Mount Washington Tunnel, and street/private-right-of-way running in the South Hills; unsourced

segments.note: Shares the Overbrook streetcar corridor's Mount Washington Tunnel-era history (see the Blue Line) as far as Overbrook Junction, then continues further out to Library. Frequency estimated, unsourced.
sources: VERIFIED 2026-08-24: the Mount Washington Transit Tunnel opened Dec 1 1904 and carried its first fare-paying passengers Dec 4 1904 — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Washington_Transit_Tunnel
Headway remains an estimate — the era boundary is verified, the service frequency is not.

segments.note: Retained by the Port Authority after 1964 as a private-right-of-way South Hills route. Frequency estimated, unsourced.
sources: VERIFIED 2026-08-24: "On March 1, 1964, the system was acquired by the newly established Port Authority of Allegheny County" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Light_Rail
Headway remains an estimate — the era boundary is verified, the service frequency is not.

segments.note: Converted to modern light rail as part of Stage I (1984-87), gaining a through route to the new Downtown Subway. Suspended in 1993 along with the rest of the Overbrook corridor pending reconstruction -- a real service gap, not a data gap -- with no direct rail service until it reopened.
sources: VERIFIED 2026-08-24: Stage I construction "began on December 10, 1980" and "the first modern light rail cars began operating on April 15, 1984" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Light_Rail
Headway remains an estimate — the era boundary is verified, the service frequency is not.

segments.note: Restored with the rebuilt Overbrook line's June 2004 reopening after 11 years closed, running as the 'Library' branch of what was then still called the Blue Line.
sources: VERIFIED 2026-08-24: "The Overbrook line reopened in June 2004" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Light_Rail
Headway remains an estimate — the era boundary is verified, the service frequency is not.

segments.note: Extended to North Side/Allegheny via the North Shore Connector (opened Mar 25 2012).
sources: VERIFIED 2026-08-24: the North Shore Connector "opened to the public on March 25, 2012, with a final cost of $523.4 million" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Light_Rail
Headway remains an estimate — the era boundary is verified, the service frequency is not.

segments.note: Redesignated the Silver Line in February/March 2020, splitting it off from the Blue Line name to reduce confusion between the two South Hills-bound services (Library vs. South Hills Village).
sources: VERIFIED 2026-08-24: the Library branch of the Blue Line was renamed the Silver Line on Mar 15 2020, to stop it being confused with the Blue Line to South Hills Village — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Line_(Pittsburgh) and https://www.post-gazette.com/local/south/2020/02/18/Port-Authority-blue-line-light-rail-Library-Station-Silver-Line-Library/stories/202002180165
Headway remains an estimate — the era boundary is verified, the service frequency is not.

Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: Per-segment verification pass 2026-08-24: 6 of 6 segment boundaries in this file are verified against the Pittsburgh Light Rail article, the Mount Washington Transit Tunnel article or the Post-Gazette report of the 2020 renaming, each quoted in the segment's own sources entry. The 1987–2012 span is an editorial division rather than a documented change, and is marked as such. What service actually ran over these specific corridors in the 1904–1964 streetcar era has not been sourced — only the tunnel's opening and the Port Authority takeover have. All headways are estimates.
